prompt: In the diagram, $OB_i$ is parallel and equal in length to $A_iA_{i+1}$ for $i = 1, 2, 3$ and $4$ ($A_5 = A_1$). Show that the area of $B_1B_2B_3B_4$ is twice that of $A_1A_2A_3A_4$.
answer: With $O$ as origin, $\mathbf b_i = \mathbf a_{i+1} - \mathbf a_i$; expanding the shoelace sum $\frac12\sum \mathbf b_i\times\mathbf b_{i+1}$ gives $2\cdot\frac12\sum\mathbf a_i\times\mathbf a_{i+1}$ because the terms $\mathbf a_i\times\mathbf a_{i+2}$ cancel.

solutions.title: Shoelace with vectors
solutions.body:
Take $O$ as the origin and write $\mathbf a_i$, $\mathbf b_i$ for the position vectors of $A_i$, $B_i$ (indices mod $4$). As in the diagram, $\overrightarrow{OB_i} = \overrightarrow{A_iA_{i+1}}$, i.e.
$$\mathbf b_i = \mathbf a_{i+1} - \mathbf a_i.$$
For plane vectors let $\mathbf p\times\mathbf q = p_xq_y - p_yq_x$. The signed area of a quadrilateral $X_1X_2X_3X_4$ is $\frac12\sum_{i=1}^4 \mathbf x_i\times\mathbf x_{i+1}$ (shoelace formula). Let $S = \frac12\sum \mathbf a_i\times\mathbf a_{i+1}$ be the signed area of $A_1A_2A_3A_4$.

Expand, using $\mathbf p\times\mathbf p = 0$:
$$\mathbf b_i\times\mathbf b_{i+1} = (\mathbf a_{i+1} - \mathbf a_i)\times(\mathbf a_{i+2} - \mathbf a_{i+1}) = \mathbf a_{i+1}\times\mathbf a_{i+2} + \mathbf a_i\times\mathbf a_{i+1} - \mathbf a_i\times\mathbf a_{i+2}.$$
Summing over $i = 1, \dots, 4$: the first two terms each sum to $2S$. The last terms are $\mathbf a_1\times\mathbf a_3 + \mathbf a_2\times\mathbf a_4 + \mathbf a_3\times\mathbf a_1 + \mathbf a_4\times\mathbf a_2 = 0$ by antisymmetry. Hence
$$\tfrac12\sum_{i=1}^4 \mathbf b_i\times\mathbf b_{i+1} = \tfrac12(2S + 2S) = 2S.$$
So the signed area of $B_1B_2B_3B_4$ is twice that of $A_1A_2A_3A_4$. For the convex quadrilateral of the diagram, the vectors $\mathbf b_i$ are its side vectors taken in order, which turn around once in the same rotational sense, so $B_1B_2B_3B_4$ is also convex with the same orientation; taking absolute values, $[B_1B_2B_3B_4] = 2[A_1A_2A_3A_4]$. ∎

solutions.title: Decompose into triangles at O
solutions.body:
$O$ lies inside $B_1B_2B_3B_4$ (the side vectors $\mathbf b_i$ of the convex quadrilateral point in four directions turning once around), so
$$[B_1B_2B_3B_4] = \sum_{i} [OB_iB_{i+1}] = \sum_i \tfrac12\left|\mathbf b_i\times\mathbf b_{i+1}\right|,$$
and $\frac12|\mathbf b_i\times\mathbf b_{i+1}|$ is the area of the triangle formed by two consecutive sides of $A_1A_2A_3A_4$, namely $[A_iA_{i+1}A_{i+2}]$. Each diagonal splits the quadrilateral into two triangles: $[A_1A_2A_3] + [A_3A_4A_1] = [A_1A_2A_3A_4]$ and $[A_2A_3A_4] + [A_4A_1A_2] = [A_1A_2A_3A_4]$. Adding,
$$[B_1B_2B_3B_4] = \sum_i [A_iA_{i+1}A_{i+2}] = 2[A_1A_2A_3A_4]. \qquad ∎$$

prompt:
If $a$, $b$ and $c$ are the roots of the equation $x^3 - x^2 - x - 1 = 0$,

(i) show that $a$, $b$ and $c$ are distinct;

(ii) show that
$$\frac{a^{1982} - b^{1982}}{a - b} + \frac{b^{1982} - c^{1982}}{b - c} + \frac{c^{1982} - a^{1982}}{c - a}$$
is an integer.
answer: (i) A repeated root would also be a root of $3x^2 - 2x - 1 = (3x+1)(x-1)$, but $x = 1, -\frac13$ are not roots. (ii) $U_n = \sum_{\text{pairs}} \frac{x^n - y^n}{x-y}$ satisfies $U_{n+3} = U_{n+2} + U_{n+1} + U_n$ with $U_0 = 0$, $U_1 = 3$, $U_2 = 2$, so every $U_n$ is an integer.

solutions.title: A linear recurrence
solutions.body:
Let $f(x) = x^3 - x^2 - x - 1$.

**(i)** A repeated root of $f$ is also a root of $f'(x) = 3x^2 - 2x - 1 = (3x+1)(x-1)$. But $f(1) = -2 \ne 0$ and $f(-\frac13) = -\frac1{27} - \frac19 + \frac13 - 1 = -\frac{22}{27} \ne 0$. So the roots are distinct.

**(ii)** For two distinct roots $x, y$ put $u_n(x,y) = \dfrac{x^n - y^n}{x - y}$. Each root satisfies $t^3 = t^2 + t + 1$, so $t^{n+3} = t^{n+2} + t^{n+1} + t^n$ for $t = x, y$ and all $n \ge 0$; subtracting and dividing by $x - y$,
$$u_{n+3} = u_{n+2} + u_{n+1} + u_n.$$
Let $U_n = u_n(a,b) + u_n(b,c) + u_n(c,a)$; note $\frac{c^n - a^n}{c - a} = u_n(c,a)$, so the expression in the problem is $U_{1982}$. $U_n$ satisfies the same recurrence, and
$$U_0 = 0, \qquad U_1 = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3, \qquad U_2 = (a+b) + (b+c) + (c+a) = 2(a+b+c) = 2,$$
using Vieta's formula $a + b + c = 1$. By induction every $U_n$ is an integer (a sum of three integers). In particular $U_{1982}$ is an integer. ∎

(The values continue $U_3 = 5$, $U_4 = 10$, $U_5 = 17$, …; a numerical check with the actual roots agrees.)

solutions.title: Symmetric polynomials
solutions.body:
$\dfrac{x^n - y^n}{x - y} = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} x^ky^{n-1-k}$ is a polynomial in $x, y$ with integer coefficients that is symmetric in $x$ and $y$. Therefore the given sum is
$$\sum_{\{x,y\}} \ \sum_{k=0}^{1981} x^ky^{1981-k},$$
summed over the three unordered pairs $\{x,y\} \subset \{a,b,c\}$; any permutation of $a, b, c$ permutes these pairs, so this is a symmetric polynomial in $a, b, c$ with integer coefficients. By the fundamental theorem on symmetric polynomials it is a polynomial with integer coefficients in $e_1 = a + b + c = 1$, $e_2 = ab + bc + ca = -1$, $e_3 = abc = 1$, hence an integer. ∎

prompt: Let $R^n$ be the $n$-dimensional Euclidean space. Determine the smallest number $g(n)$ of points of a set in $R^n$ such that every point in $R^n$ is at irrational distance from at least one point in that set.

solutions.title: Lower bounds and a median-formula construction
solutions.body:
**One point never suffices**: the point itself is at distance $0$ (rational) from it. So $g(n) \ge 2$.

**$n = 1$: two points suffice.** Take $0$ and $\sqrt2$. If some real $x$ had rational distances $|x|$ and $|x - \sqrt2|$ to both, then $\sqrt2 = \pm|x| \pm |x - \sqrt2|$ would be rational. So $g(1) = 2$.

**$n \ge 2$: two points never suffice.** Given $A \ne B$, choose a rational $q > \frac12|AB|$. In a plane through $A$ and $B$, the circles with centres $A$, $B$ and radius $q$ meet (since $q + q > |AB|$ and $|q - q| < |AB|$), giving a point at rational distance $q$ from both. (If $A = B$, any point at rational distance from $A$ works.) So $g(n) \ge 3$.

**$n \ge 2$: three points suffice.** Let $\alpha = \sqrt[4]{2}$, so $\alpha^2 = \sqrt2$ is irrational, and take three collinear points $A$, $B$, $C$ with $B$ the midpoint of $AC$ and $AB = BC = \alpha$. For any point $X$ (in any dimension), the median formula (Apollonius)
$$XA^2 + XC^2 = 2XB^2 + 2\alpha^2$$
holds. [Proof: with $B$ as origin, $C = -A$, $|X - A|^2 + |X + A|^2 = 2|X|^2 + 2|A|^2$.] If $XA$, $XB$, $XC$ were all rational, then $\alpha^2 = \frac12(XA^2 + XC^2) - XB^2$ would be rational — a contradiction. So every point is at irrational distance from one of $A$, $B$, $C$.

**Answer: $g(1) = 2$, and $g(n) = 3$ for all $n \ge 2$.** ∎

prompt: Let $p$ be a permutation of the set $S_n = \{1, 2, \dots, n\}$. An element $j \in S_n$ is called a *fixed point* of $p$ if $p(j) = j$. Let $f_n$ be the number of permutations having no fixed points, and $g_n$ be the number with exactly one fixed point. Show that $|f_n - g_n| = 1$.
answer: $g_n = n f_{n-1}$ (choose the fixed point, derange the rest) and $f_n = n f_{n-1} + (-1)^n$, so $f_n - g_n = (-1)^n$.

solutions.title: Inclusion–exclusion
solutions.body:
Let $f_0 = 1$ (the empty permutation has no fixed points).

**$g_n = n f_{n-1}$.** A permutation with exactly one fixed point is obtained by choosing the fixed point $j$ ($n$ ways) and a permutation of the other $n-1$ elements without fixed points ($f_{n-1}$ ways), and each arises exactly once.

**Formula for $f_n$.** For $j \in S_n$ let $E_j$ be the set of permutations fixing $j$. A permutation fixing a given set of $k$ elements is a permutation of the remaining $n-k$, so $|E_{j_1}\cap\cdots\cap E_{j_k}| = (n-k)!$. By inclusion–exclusion,
$$f_n = \sum_{k=0}^{n} (-1)^k\binom nk (n-k)! = n!\sum_{k=0}^n \frac{(-1)^k}{k!}.$$
Hence, for $n \ge 1$,
$$f_n - n f_{n-1} = n!\sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{(-1)^k}{k!} - n\cdot(n-1)!\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\frac{(-1)^k}{k!} = n!\cdot\frac{(-1)^n}{n!} = (-1)^n.$$

Therefore $f_n - g_n = f_n - nf_{n-1} = (-1)^n$, and $|f_n - g_n| = 1$. ∎

(E.g. $f_4 = 9$, $g_4 = 8$; $f_5 = 44$, $g_5 = 45$.)

solutions.title: Recurrence
solutions.body:
The classical recurrence $f_n = (n-1)(f_{n-1} + f_{n-2})$ for $n \ge 2$ holds. In a derangement $p$ of $S_n$ let $k = p(n)$ ($n-1$ choices). If $p(k) = n$, deleting $n$ and $k$ leaves a derangement of the other $n-2$ elements, and conversely; this gives $f_{n-2}$ derangements for each $k$. If $p(k) \ne n$, let $j = p^{-1}(n)$ (so $j \ne k$) and define $q$ on $S_{n-1}$ by $q(j) = k$ and $q(i) = p(i)$ otherwise; $q$ is a derangement of $S_{n-1}$ with $q^{-1}(k) = j$, and conversely every derangement $q$ of $S_{n-1}$ arises from exactly one such $p$ (put $j = q^{-1}(k)$, $p(j) = n$, $p(n) = k$). This gives $f_{n-1}$ derangements for each $k$.

Let $d_n = f_n - nf_{n-1}$ ($= f_n - g_n$). From the recurrence,
$$d_n = (n-1)f_{n-1} + (n-1)f_{n-2} - nf_{n-1} = -\bigl(f_{n-1} - (n-1)f_{n-2}\bigr) = -d_{n-1}.$$
With $d_1 = f_1 - 1\cdot f_0 = 0 - 1 = -1$ we get $d_n = (-1)^n$, so $|f_n - g_n| = 1$. ∎

prompt: The altitudes of a tetrahedron $ABCD$ are extended externally to points $A'$, $B'$, $C'$ and $D'$ respectively, where $AA' = k/h_a$, $BB' = k/h_b$, $CC' = k/h_c$ and $DD' = k/h_d$. Here, $k$ is a constant and $h_a$ denotes the length of the altitude of $ABCD$ from vertex $A$, *etc.* Prove that the centroid of the tetrahedron $A'B'C'D'$ coincides with the centroid of $ABCD$.
answer: $\overrightarrow{AA'} = \frac{k}{h_a}\mathbf u_a = -\frac{k}{3V}S_a\mathbf N_a$ (with $S_a$ the area and $\mathbf N_a$ the outward unit normal of the face opposite $A$), and the outward area vectors of a closed tetrahedron sum to $\mathbf 0$, so $\sum \overrightarrow{AA'} = \mathbf 0$.

solutions.title: Area vectors sum to zero
solutions.body:
The centroid of a tetrahedron is the average of its four vertices, so we must show
$$\overrightarrow{AA'} + \overrightarrow{BB'} + \overrightarrow{CC'} + \overrightarrow{DD'} = \mathbf 0.$$

Let $V$ be the volume, $S_a$ the area of the face $BCD$ opposite $A$, and $\mathbf N_a$ the unit normal of that face pointing **out** of the tetrahedron (similarly for $b, c, d$). The altitude from $A$ is perpendicular to face $BCD$, and extending it externally beyond $A$ means moving away from that face, i.e. in the direction $-\mathbf N_a$. Since $V = \frac13 S_a h_a$, we have $\frac{1}{h_a} = \frac{S_a}{3V}$ and
$$\overrightarrow{AA'} = \frac{k}{h_a}(-\mathbf N_a) = -\frac{k}{3V}\,S_a\mathbf N_a.$$
So it suffices to prove $S_a\mathbf N_a + S_b\mathbf N_b + S_c\mathbf N_c + S_d\mathbf N_d = \mathbf 0$.

**Lemma.** For any tetrahedron, the four outward area vectors sum to $\mathbf 0$.

*Proof.* Put $A$ at the origin and let $\mathbf b, \mathbf c, \mathbf d$ be the position vectors of $B, C, D$; let $\Delta = \mathbf b\cdot(\mathbf c\times\mathbf d) \ne 0$. Consider
$$\mathbf v_D = \tfrac12\,\mathbf b\times\mathbf c,\quad \mathbf v_B = \tfrac12\,\mathbf c\times\mathbf d,\quad \mathbf v_C = \tfrac12\,\mathbf d\times\mathbf b,\quad \mathbf v_A = \tfrac12(\mathbf d - \mathbf b)\times(\mathbf c - \mathbf b),$$
normal to the faces $ABC$, $ACD$, $ADB$, $BCD$ respectively, each of length equal to the area of its face. Expanding, $(\mathbf d - \mathbf b)\times(\mathbf c - \mathbf b) = \mathbf d\times\mathbf c - \mathbf d\times\mathbf b - \mathbf b\times\mathbf c$, so
$$\mathbf v_A = -\tfrac12\left(\mathbf b\times\mathbf c + \mathbf c\times\mathbf d + \mathbf d\times\mathbf b\right) = -(\mathbf v_D + \mathbf v_B + \mathbf v_C), \qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad \mathbf v_A + \mathbf v_B + \mathbf v_C + \mathbf v_D = \mathbf 0.$$
They all point outward or all inward: $\mathbf v_D$ is outward iff it points away from $D$, i.e. $\mathbf v_D\cdot\mathbf d < 0$, i.e. $\Delta < 0$; similarly $\mathbf v_B\cdot\mathbf b = \frac12\Delta$ and $\mathbf v_C\cdot\mathbf c = \frac12\Delta$; and $\mathbf v_A$ is outward iff $\mathbf v_A\cdot(\mathbf 0 - \mathbf b) < 0$, where $\mathbf v_A\cdot(-\mathbf b) = \frac12(\mathbf b\times\mathbf c + \mathbf c\times\mathbf d + \mathbf d\times\mathbf b)\cdot\mathbf b = \frac12\Delta$. So all four have the same orientation, and $\sum S_x\mathbf N_x = \pm\sum\mathbf v_X = \mathbf 0$. $\square$

Hence $\sum \overrightarrow{XX'} = -\frac{k}{3V}\sum S_x\mathbf N_x = \mathbf 0$, so $\frac14(A' + B' + C' + D') = \frac14(A + B + C + D)$: the two tetrahedra have the same centroid. ∎
